content_html:
Archaeology reconstructs human history through the material remains of past societies. From stone tools and cave paintings to monumental architecture and written texts, the archaeological record spans over 300,000 years of human existence and provides the only direct evidence for how our ancestors lived, thought, and organized themselves.

Human Origins and Prehistory

The study of human evolution draws on fossil evidence, genetic analysis, and archaeological excavations across Africa, Europe, and Asia. Key questions include the timing and routes of human migration out of Africa, the interaction between Homo sapiens and Neanderthals, and the cognitive and cultural developments that enabled the emergence of complex societies.

Classical Civilizations

The classical world of Greece, Rome, Egypt, and Mesopotamia produced enduring achievements in philosophy, literature, law, and engineering. The Villa of the Papyri in Herculaneum, buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, preserves the only intact library from classical antiquity. AI-driven virtual unwrapping is now recovering lost philosophical works that have not been read in nearly 2,000 years.

Digital Archaeology and New Methods

Modern archaeology increasingly relies on non-destructive technologies including ground-penetrating radar, LiDAR, satellite imagery, and CT scanning. These tools allow researchers to discover and analyze sites without excavation, preserving them for future generations while extracting unprecedented amounts of data from existing artifacts and structures.
